\subsection{Retrieval exposure and natural-retrieval outcomes (RQ1)}
Retrieval-only calibration showed that one inserted document was exposed much more often for public-standard items than for fictional asset-specific items. Table~\ref{tab:stagea} reports Poison@$k$ at $k=5$.

\midrule

Despite this exposure, exact attacker-value adoption remained low. With one poison, Tier~1 ASR was 2.9--2.9\% and Tier~2 ASR was 0.0--0.0\%. With three poisons, Tier~1 ASR was 2.9--2.9\% and Tier~2 ASR was 3.3--4.4\% across models.

Poison-last contexts produced 0\% correct-answer retention for all three models and both tiers; responses instead declined to commit because the final passage contradicted the preceding majority. Poison-first retention varied substantially by model and tier, showing a position effect without attacker-value adoption.

At 70\% record coverage, D3 reduced SVR by 3.1--3.8 percentage points across models; at 100\% coverage the reduction was 3.8--5.0 points. All planned Holm-adjusted McNemar tests were non-significant ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=1.0$), so the bootstrap effect-size intervals are interpreted descriptively.
\subsection{Legitimate-conflict cost}
D3 can reject a correct context-specific answer when the simplified structured record lacks the applicable jurisdictional or interconnection variant. BFFR is therefore computed only among Tier~3 trials for which clean RAG first returned the benchmark-correct answer.

The coverage benefit therefore has a clear cost: at 70\% coverage BFFR was about 43.6--45.7\%, and at full coverage it was about 64.1--65.7\%.
